extracted.intended_audience: aspiring courtiers, gentlemen, and attendants at Renaissance-style courts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for the ideal Courtier's behaviour, conversation, dress, and public conduct—how to make favorable impressions, use wit, avoid vices, and display accomplishments with discretion. Drawn from a Renaissance conduct manual aimed at gentlemen seeking success at court.

rubrics_metrics.name: First impressions matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courtier ought to take great care to make a good impression at the start, because first impressions have very great weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of initial appearance and behaviour: reputation and early conduct shape others' expectations long-term. The text gives anecdotal proof (ladies falling in love upon hearing another praise a man) to show how a strong first impression spreads and endures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid raising unrealistic expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not raise such expectations or send fame before you; the mind often imagines things it is impossible to fulfil, and thus we lose more than we gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from boasting or allowing exaggerated reputation to circulate; inflated reputation invites disappointment when the reality is measured against imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation must be justified by acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A Courtier's reputation should be confirmed by his acts — confidence in reputation is hourly confirmed when acts justify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate real accomplishments rather than relying on hearsay. Let behaviour and performance validate any praise you receive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse, indecent, or vulgar pleasantries
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not utter the foulest and most indecent things before honourable ladies or use pleasantries that make them blush; such behaviour is folly and shameful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain decorum in mixed company. Anti-patterns include indecent jokes, crude language, and intentionally making respectable company uncomfortable to seem jovial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shun rough practical jokes and dangerous antics
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid boorish physical jests—throwing people down stairs, clapping wood/bricks on backs, casting dust in eyes, making horses run into ditches, or flinging food—these are not marks of a good Courtier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse raucous, physical 'amusements' with courtly wit; such behaviour provokes disgust rather than admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in eating, drinking, and habits
rubrics_metrics.description: A Courtier ought not to avow himself a great eater or drinker or be given to excess or vile ungoverned life; such habits disqualify a man from courtly business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep personal habits temperate and avoid peasant or rustic behaviours that clash with courtly expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know several accomplishments but be discreet about them
rubrics_metrics.description: A Courtier should know what befits him so that every possible thing may be easy to him and everyone may marvel at him, yet he should avoid lofty indifference and not appear to think himself superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop multiple skills (arms, languages, arts) but present them with modesty; praise others and avoid disparaging silence. Appear ready and prepared but act as if accidental or requested rather than ostentatious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showcase strengths, touch lightly on mediocrity, confess true ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: When he excels in something, the Courtier should attract notice subtly; in things where he is mediocre he should touch lightly, and where wholly ignorant he should not pretend but confess ignorance if compelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish and stage your strengths without ostentation. Do not feign competence; if forced to display ignorance, be frank rather than risk exposure. Avoid unnecessarily volunteering self-deprecations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid boasting, lying or extreme exaggeration in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against getting the name of a liar or a boaster; in talk, do not go beyond the probable nor tell truths that have the look of falsehood; avoid extravagant vows of friendship or extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speak within credible bounds. Anti-patterns include extravagant oaths, melodramatic farewells, or habitual recounting of miracles to claim authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise decorous discretion to avoid envy
rubrics_metrics.description: Govern yourself with a certain decorous discretion, which is a strong shield against envy; avoid ostentation that breeds envy or suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance visibility and restraint. Use modesty and measured praise of others to minimize ill will and envy at court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise others kindly; avoid haughty indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not show lofty, ungenial indifference or disparage others by silence; instead praise fine achievements of others with kindness and good will while appearing modest about your own worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate gracious comportment: acknowledge others' merits and avoid behaviour that implies no one equals you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready and prepared but act as if impromptu
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him if possible come ready and prepared, yet appearing to act impromptu throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation gives grace; affect ease and spontaneity so accomplishments seem natural, not manufactured. This is considered an artful embellishment rather than deceit if done with judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use wit and pleasantries suited to person, place, and occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasantries and witticisms must consider the kind of person with whom one speaks, the place, the occasion, and the soberness and modesty that ought to be maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate types of wit: long humorous narrative (urbane style) vs short biting sayings (apothegms/argusie). Match tone and formality to the audience; avoid overloquacity that becomes silly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know limits of derision and whom to ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the bounds and limits of exciting laughter by derision: do not jeer at the poor or at open blackguards, nor at universally beloved or powerful people; rather scorn vices of those neither pitiable nor dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derision should target appropriate incongruities and not expose you to dangerous enmities or appear cruel. The laughable springs from incongruity, but exercise prudence in targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish natural wit with judgment and art
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature and intellect create men fitted to be witty, but judgment and art polish and correct conceits, culling the good and rejecting the bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate innate gifts through practice and refinement. Even spontaneous-seeming argutiae benefit from cultivated taste and avoidance of ill-conceived remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation or badly copied foreign manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not clumsily copy the mannerisms of other nations (e.g., trying to be 'good Frenchmen' when not bred there); affected gestures and mannerisms look ill-fitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt manners that suit your natural bearing and culture; imitation that is inauthentic appears ludicrous and undermine courtly grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn useful foreign languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing many languages (especially Spanish and French) is approved in the Courtier because intercourse with those nations is frequent and necessary for conversation at court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquire languages that enable diplomatic and social interchange; linguistic competence increases utility and esteem at international courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrating shameful incidents or repeating disgrace
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not needlessly recount events that imply disgrace (e.g., tales of flight, falling, or being cudgelled) so as not to invite ridicule; avoid self-accusal of your own accord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer conversation away from recounting one's humiliations. Self-deprecatory stories that invite contempt are harmful to reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abandon your chief art for another in which you are mediocre
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who abandon their primary art to pursue another in which they are ignorant often make themselves ridiculous and lose their first skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate and preserve your true profession and core accomplishments; avoid chasing fashions that undermine your proven reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to amuse reasonably and gracefully — laughter arises from incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything that moves to laughter cheers the mind and gives pleasure; laughter springs from incongruity — things that seem amiss without being so — and should be elicited reasonably and with grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comic effect to refresh and relieve company, but keep it tasteful, proportionate, and bounded by decorum. The goal is recreation, not derision or cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use artful concealment (wary dissimulation) sparingly and justly
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not unseemly for a man conscious of doing something well to seek occasions to show it and at the same time to conceal what he thinks undeserving of praise — but with a touch of wary dissimulation and good judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame self-promotion as modesty or chance, not as blatant display; compare to tasteful setting of a jewel. Beware crossing into deceit that invites censure.
